title: Cheapest AND Walk Between Nodes
statement:
An undirected graph has n nodes, 0 to n − 1. Each edges[i] = [u, v, w] joins u and v with weight w. Two nodes may be joined by several edges.

A walk is any sequence of edges where each edge starts where the previous one ended. Unlike a path, a walk may repeat nodes and edges as often as it likes. The cost of a walk is the bitwise AND of the weights of all the edges it uses.

For each queries[j] = [s, t] with s ≠ t, find the smallest cost of any walk from s to t, or -1 if no walk exists. Return the answers in query order.

examples.why: The direct edge 0–2 costs 13, but the walk 0 → 1 → 2 → 0 → 2 uses all three edges: 7 AND 5 AND 13 = 5. Node 3 has no edges.
Walking 0 → 1 → 2 → 1 takes the 10 edge as a detour past the target: 12 AND 10 = 8, cheaper than 12.

hints: AND can only clear bits, never set them. So does taking one more edge ever make a walk more expensive?
Since a walk may go anywhere and come back, a walk from s to t can use every edge of their connected component. That is the cheapest possible walk.
Group nodes into components with union-find and keep, for each component, the AND of all its edge weights. A query is -1 if s and t are in different components, otherwise that component's AND.

explain.intuition:
Shortest-path thinking is a trap here. AND only ever turns bits off: x AND w ≤ x for any w. So adding an edge to a walk never raises its cost, and the cheapest walk wants to use as many edges as possible.

Walks may repeat edges, so from s you can wander to every edge in the connected component, cross it, come back, and finish at t. That walk uses every edge in the component, which is the minimum possible cost. So the whole problem collapses to: which component is each node in, and what is the AND of all edge weights in that component? Union-find answers both in nearly O(1) per operation.
steps: Create a union-find over the n nodes. Give each root an AND value of all ones (for example -1).
For each edge [u, v, w]: union u and v, combining the two AND values, then AND w into the new root's value.
For each query: if find(s) ≠ find(t), answer -1. Otherwise answer the AND value stored at their root.
pitfalls: Running a shortest-path search. Fewer edges is not cheaper here; more edges is.
Only AND-ing the edges seen after a union, and losing the values that were stored at the root that got merged away.
Answering 0 for disconnected nodes because the AND value was initialised to 0 instead of all ones.

solutions.title: Explore the component for every query
solutions.idea: For each query, BFS from s over the whole component, AND every edge weight met, and check whether t was reached.

solutions.title: Union-find with an AND per component
solutions.idea: A walk can cover every edge of its component, so the answer is the AND of the whole component. Union-find tracks both membership and that AND.

followups: Queries may have s = t. What is the cost of an empty walk, and when should you return it?
The cost is the bitwise OR instead. Which walks are best now, and why does the problem become much harder?
